title: AP Pittman
text:
Hi! I’m AP (they/them), a Sociology Ph.D. candidate at Duke. My scholarship is organized around two central questions: why do U.S. states enact and enforce some policies instead of others, and how does the enforcement of those policies impact population health in both intended and unintended ways?
Links to my CV and Github are below; you can also find more information on my research and teaching by following the links in the header.

title: Research
text: My research to date treats U.S. states as sites where institutions and policy choices produce unequal outcomes. In a solo-authored paper under review at SSM - Population Health, I use two-way fixed effects models to test whether gerrymandering is associated with infant mortality, and find that a one-standard-deviation increase in the gerrymandering measure corresponds to increases in Black, White, and total rates of infant mortality. In another working paper, I use difference-in-differences methods to study Ohio’s 2023 abortion-protection amendment; preliminary results show that it was associated with a significant reduction of anxiety and depressive symptoms among women. A third working paper examines how anti-trans laws affect the mental health of trans and gender non-conforming (TGNC) people using staggered difference-in-differences models, and finds that the first anti-trans law to pass in a state was associated with an increase in symptoms of anxiety and depression among its TGNC residents compared to TGNC residents of states which had not yet passed an anti-trans law.

title: Research
text:
Collaborative Projects
My research program is interdisciplinary, and as such, I have sought out many interdisciplinary partnerships while at Duke. One of the main locations in which I do collaborative research currently is in the Research in Sexual and Gender Minority Equity (RISE) Lab under Dr. Tonia Poteat in Duke’s School of Nursing. I am co-first author on a paper under review at Health Psychology & Behavioral Medicine that uses structural equation modeling to assess the mediating role of stress in the relationship between experiences of discrimination and mental health problems for Black and Latina trans women living with HIV. I am also first author on a paper in progress that qualitatively examines the experiences of trans and gender non-conforming participants in a study investigating the impact of financial resources on physical and mental health; the manuscript will be the culmination of over a year’s work conducting nearly 70 in-depth interviews and analyzing responses. The other main source of collaboration for me is my participation in Dr. Hedwig Lee’s research group at Duke. As part of this lab, I am first author on a paper under review at Population Research and Policy Review that examines state-level race-specific trends in probation, parole, and imprisonment, and corresponding changes in infant mortality rates. In addition, I am first author on a paper soon to be submitted which investigates heterogeneity in Black birth outcomes following the police-involved killing of Amadou Diallo in the Bronx in 1999, and a main contributor to another paper which attempts to classify states into regimes of incarceration and probation and map how those regimes have changed over time using sequence analysis. My work in these research teams has allowed me to work with sociologists, epidemiologists, nurse scientists, physicians, and demographers, and that interdisciplinarity has shaped my own scholarship. It has also kept me grounded in the fact that the broad social and societal phenomena that we study as sociologists can have profound impacts on the health of populations through processes such as healthcare delivery, utilization of healthcare services, and patient decision-making.

title: Research
text:
Future Directions
My research agenda moving forward is dedicated to understanding how states act to regulate certain bodies, and the consequences of these regulations for populations, population health, and healthcare service delivery. Over the next phase of my career, I will address the following questions:

How do recent diverging trends in state laws and law enforcement, particularly laws that regulate what form bodies can take and where bodies can go (exemplified by the rise of anti-trans laws, the proliferation of abortion bans, increased pregnancy criminalization, increases in community supervision with stabilizing rates of incarceration, varying levels of cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, etc.) interact to reproduce intra- and inter-state inequalities by race, gender, and class?
What are the consequences of these trends for fertility, mortality, and population health?

title: Teaching
text:
I have been involved with teaching more than ten courses over the past eight years, in roles ranging from undergraduate teaching associate to instructor of record, in addition to my mentorship and teaching experiences outside the traditional classroom. In my undergraduate years, I was an undergraduate associate for introductory Sociology at Miami University under Dr. Jen Bulanda. As part of my involvement in the course, I helped to design, implement, and evaluate changes to the introductory sociology curriculum; I also learned how to facilitate team-based learning and flipped-classroom approaches in an introductory sociology context. During my MGS coursework at Miami, I was involved with teaching SOC/GTY 318 (Social Forces and Aging) – first as a TA under Dr. J. Scott Brown, and then as the instructor of record the following semester. It was a trial-by-fire for my first semester teaching solo, as it also happened to be the Fall semester of 2020, but the experience in syllabus-building, lecturing, and facilitating class discussions was perhaps even more salient for being situated in the still-new Zoom classroom world of the COVID pandemic.
At Duke, I’ve TAed for courses like Technology and Organizations, Medical Sociology, and the Sociology of Mental Health. As part of my TA responsibilities, I’ve often given guest lectures in class and provided supplemental learning materials for students that emphasized my subfield expertise. I also have given invited guest lectures to classes as small as 20 students and as large as 150 students, connecting my own expertise in population health and mental health to coursework in the Sociology and African & African American Studies departments. My experiences with teaching and curriculum-building continued in my position as a 2025-26 Constellations Fellow, in which I was responsible for designing experiential learning activities, digital community spaces, and formative assessments for Duke’s new first-year liberal arts curriculum. It allowed me to experience a higher level of education administration, managing both students’ and faculty members’ needs and expectations around the new curriculum. This birds-eye view of teaching at a preeminent undergraduate institution will serve me well as a new faculty member. Finally, this year I am serving as a fellow in the Program for Advanced Research in the Social Sciences through Duke’s Social Science Research Institute; my responsibilities include creating research skills workshops for thesis-writing undergraduates and providing research support to undergraduates, graduates, postdocs, and faculty members in all stages of research, from constructing a research question to polishing a manuscript.

title: Teaching
text:
My Approach to Pedagogy
I have sought out many resources to improve my teaching, from full-length graduate pedagogy courses to many workshops and mini-courses, culminating in the Certificate in College Teaching through Duke’s Graduate School. Through the past eight years of experience, I’ve had ample opportunity to refine and strengthen my teaching approach. I use the following three tenets to guide my approach to constructing and teaching all courses.

Invest time and energy creating a shared knowledge base.

In my experience as an instructor, a TA, and a mentor, I’ve found that the easiest way to lose a class is by failing to spend enough time at the beginning establishing a shared base of knowledge. To avoid this in my own teaching, I make a point of starting slow and ensuring understanding of basic concepts before moving on to more complex topics. I’ve found that investing time into the basics, even when they may seem like review to some students, pays off heavily later in the course. In statistics-based courses, this may look like reviewing basic tenets of probability theory and calculus before attempting to teach alpha levels, or spending time explaining how R and RStudio work together using your computer’s file system before attempting to teach a coding language. In content-based courses, this may look like explaining how journal articles are laid out before assigning one to be read, or reminding students about the distinction between agency and structure before teaching about institutionalized racism.
This principle holds even in smaller-scale teaching: I’ve used it in guest lectures I’ve given to Sociology and African American Studies classes at Duke, as well as in mini-seminars I led about research skills for undergraduates. I spend a few minutes at the beginning reviewing the basics before delving into my expertise, ensuring that all the students have a foothold before moving on. This helps all students, even if they don’t “need” the foothold: in my own life as a student and researcher in classes and conferences, I’ve found that hearing the same topic introduced multiple times by different people can help me triangulate my own opinions and beliefs on the topic. Exposing students to core concepts multiple times in different contexts will help us produce thoughtful, informed, and opinionated sociologists.

Design and teach courses with accessibility in mind.

Accessibility is a core value of mine, inside and outside of the teaching sphere. As someone who made it through college and two master’s degrees before being diagnosed with ADHD, making my classroom meaningfully accessible for students without them having to ask for accommodations is a core teaching value that’s informed by my own experience. Specifically, I am guided by the disability studies concept of Universal Design for Learning (UDL; see Ralabate, 2011), which holds that by designing our courses with accessibility as a central tenet, we will make the course better for everyone, regardless of their disability status. The principles of UDL boil down to providing multiple ways of learning, engaging with, and expressing the key concepts in a class.
When teaching and planning courses, I create content geared toward different learning styles which approaches each topic from several directions. When I taught a class titled “Social Forces and Aging” in 2020, I included an “aging in the media” assignment, which asked small groups of students to find examples of aging portrayed in film, TV, music, or ads and prepare a short presentation for the rest of the class. Those presentations took the first 5-10 minutes of class for the rest of the semester, and they emphasized several different kinds of learning (auditory, kinesthetic, visual) in a way that traditional lectures could not, while allowing students to take ownership of their learning. They also sparked discussion and laughter in the class, which helped set the tone for the course. This assignment was included in the syllabus in addition to traditional lectures and readings on aging in the media, so that students could see and understand the material from as many angles as possible. I think the “ageism in the media” assignment – true to the promise of UDL – helped all of the students, regardless of their learning styles, understand aging in a more complete way than they would have through the lectures alone.

Be willing to grow and change.

Circumstances of teaching change semester to semester and even week to week, as we’ve all experienced lately. A salient example of this for me is the fact that the height of the COVID-19 pandemic happened to coincide with my first semester as a solo instructor. Although it obviously brought challenges, it also brought opportunities – what better way to teach about age vs. period vs. cohort effects than to encourage students to imagine the possible age, period, and cohort effects of the global pandemic we were living through? Even in less extreme cases, one of the best things about teaching sociology is that the world provides a plethora of relevant examples for us to use in our classes; keeping references current, in my experience, helps with both student engagement and course quality. Pivoting well also involves responding to student feedback. I always include midsemester evaluations in my courses, which allow students to give real-time feedback on the structure of the class and propose improvements. Because my classes tend to be structured similarly week-to-week, changes suggested in these evaluations – an extra day to write a weekly reflection, perhaps, or more time at the end of class for freeform discussion – can be implemented immediately without waiting for the next semester.
